newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigerian troops in Sierra Leone after coup.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian troops in Sierra Leone after coup.

text.p: Three Nigerian naval boats with troops docked in Sierra Leone on Tuesday after a coup in Freetown toppled president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, witnesses said.
Kabbah's U.N. envoy James Jonah said the ousted leader had requested help from West African states to "restore democracy" after the weekend coup led by Major Johnny Paul Koromah.
Jonah said he had been authorised to go to next week's Organisation of African Unity summit in the Zimbabwean capital Harare to ask for sanctions against the coup leaders.
These would include non-recognition of their government and a travel ban on the junior officers who organised the revolt.

Asked if Kabbah, now in Guinea, had asked for troops to oust the coup plotters, he said: "If possible yes, because what else do we have in the country. We have a bunch of corporals who opened the prisons wide open and 600 people came out, criminals and they are roaming the streets right now."
He said the West African bloc ECOWAS was committed to restoring "the legitimate government of Sierra Leone", but added "how they are going to do it I do not know".

Nigerian troops are the backbone of the ECOMOG regional force policing Liberia since shortly after civil war erupted there in 1989. Nigerian ECOMOG units protecting key sites in Sierra Leone because of civil war there were caught in battles with the coup soldiers.
Earlier on Tuesday Nigerian troops reinforced Sierra Leone's international airport and the coup leaders expressed concern about talk of a Nigerian counter-attack.
Hours later a Nigerian vessel with combat troops docked at Freetown's Government Wharf near Sierra Leone's naval base. Two others followed later in the afternoon, diplomats said.
Port and military sources in Liberia said on Monday peacekeepers left in naval boats and overland for Freetown.

"The AFRC is concerned over rumours that our brothers, the Nigerian force, are about to launch an attack," said a statement from Koromah, chairman of the newly formed Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC).

"The AFRC is hereby informing the general public to know that it is a baseless rumour. The situation is under control, and all and sundry are hereby requested to go about their normal duties," said the statement, broadcast on national radio.
Hundreds of people crammed into Freetown hotels for safety as soldiers looted homes and offices and careered round the city in stolen cars.
The German Foreign Ministry recommended that all Germans in Sierra Leone should leave. Germany joined a growing number of countries condemning the coup as a serious blow for democracy in West Africa.

Lebanon sent a Boeing 707 plane in the hope of evacuating its citizens. The Middle East Airlines plane, with a 150-person capacity, flew to Lagos, sources at Beirut airport said. It was then due to fly to Accra where it would wait for permission to fly to Freetown.

Two Lebanese citizens were killed and two wounded in coup violence in Freetown. Many of the 2,000 Lebanese living in Sierra Leone, most of them businessmen, took shelter at the Lebanese embassy in Freetown but were suffering from shortages of food and water, Foreign Minister Faris Bouez said.

Police reported protests against the coup in the southern second city of Bo, where the Kamajor civilian militia loyal to Kabbah was ignoring an order to disband. There were also clashes between troops and Kamajors in the eastern town of Daru.
The new army rulers said they had reopened the land borders and air and sea ports. A dusk to dawn curfew remained in force.

Staff at Freetown's Connaught hospital said at least 40 people had been killed in Sunday's fighting, including two Nigerians and several Sierra Leonean soldiers, but ECOMOG Field Commander General Victor Malu said in Lagos on Monday there had been no Nigerian casualties.
The hospital had treated more than 80 wounded.

Shops, banks, schools and markets remained closed on Tuesday despite the coup leaders' appeals to people to return to work. Only a few roadside traders ventured out. The coup leaders ordered civil servants to report for work immediately.
